speciesText.name: Blackspotted puffer (dogface puffer)
marks: Rounded body with a blunt, doglike snout and small mouth
Irregular black spots scatter across the body; dark patches surround the eyes and snout
Small side fins and short fins near the back of the body propel a mostly steady body
Fine prickles cover the skin rather than long, obvious spines
speciesText.role: Feeds on reef invertebrates, including corals, sponges, molluscs and tunicates, as well as algae.
speciesText.fact: Individuals may be grey, brown or partly yellow. Look for several field marks together: body colour alone cannot identify this puffer.

marineProfile.habitat: Coastal and outer reefs across the Indo-Pacific, especially areas rich in attached invertebrates. Fishes of Australia lists a 3–25 m depth range.
marineProfile.diet: Coral tissue, sponges, molluscs, tunicates and algae.
marineProfile.behavior: Small side, back and belly fins work together during steady swimming. The tail contributes more during faster bursts.
marineProfile.observe: Check the pale bar across the snout, then compare its fine skin prickles with the porcupinefish's longer spines. Watch the fins while the rounded body stays comparatively still.

evidence.nameAndStatus: California Academy Catalog verifies valid name and LC (2014). Direct IUCN page returned 403. The year 2014 is publication year, not assessment date; FishBase reports assessed 7 June 2011.
evidence.morphology: FoA Summary/Features supports marks 2 and 4 and colour variation; Australian Museum identification supports pale snout bar and shape. Mark 1 shape is also evident in museum photographs.
evidence.ecology: FoA Distribution/Feeding/Quick Facts supports habitat, 3–25 m, diet and role. Do not claim exclusive coral diet.
evidence.movement: Gordon et al. (1996) directly filmed A. nigropunctatus: pectorals 180 degrees out of phase, dorsal/anal in phase, body slightly mouth-up; tail bursts at high speed. Supports mark 3 and behavior.

model.note: Museum gives 25 cm; FoA 30 cm. 0.25 m is illustrative, not species maximum. Tiny spinules, no long porcupine spines.

speciesText.name: Ocellated eagle ray (whitespotted eagle ray)
marks: Broad diamond-shaped disc with pointed, winglike pectoral fins
Pale spots cover the dark grey-green back; the underside is white
A projecting, flattened snout forms a single duckbill shape
A thin whip tail trails far behind the disc, with small spines near its base
speciesText.role: A bottom-feeding predator of molluscs and crustaceans that searches sandy areas near reefs.
speciesText.fact: This Indo-Pacific species was once grouped with Aetobatus narinari. That name now refers to an Atlantic species, so location matters when reading older eagle-ray accounts.

marineProfile.habitat: Coastal and offshore Indo-Pacific waters, often near coral reefs, lagoons and sandy feeding grounds. Australian fisheries accounts record it from the surface to about 40 m.
marineProfile.diet: Mostly hard-shelled molluscs and crabs, with other small bottom-dwelling animals.
marineProfile.behavior: Cruises alone or in groups and digs in sand for food. Researchers have also documented occasional resting and visits from cleaner fishes.
marineProfile.observe: Compare the pointed wings and single duckbill snout with the manta's paired head lobes. Use an underside view to find the mouth and five gill slits on each side.

evidence.nameAndStatus: FoA verifies accepted Indo-Pacific name distinct from Atlantic A. narinari. EN (2024) verified by Araujo (2024), Introduction/reference 15, and official IUCN 2024 change table indexed row VU→EN. Direct IUCN page was inaccessible; table direct open returned 403. Older FoA/SAFS VU superseded.
evidence.morphology: FoA Summary/Features/Colour supports marks, gills, tail and teeth. Study prompts compare documented anatomy with existing manta entry; no paired cephalic lobes on eagle ray.
evidence.ecology: FoA Feeding supports diet and role; Distribution supports groups and habitat. SAFS Habitat and biology supports 0–40 m; FoA lists 0–60 m, so copy clearly attributes the narrower published range.
evidence.behavior: FoA supports grouping/digging; Araujo (2024) reports eight resting cases, some with cleaner fish. Occasional avoids claiming common resting.

model.note: Ratios from FoA Features citing White et al. (2010). Table 1 of Araujo (2024) includes visually estimated 1.5 m disc-width animals. Tail length may vary through damage; do not interpret the fixed ratio as a maximum. Ignore inconsistent FoA Quick Facts 153 cm total length.

Gordon, M.S., Plaut, I. and Kim, D. (1996). How puffers (Teleostei: Tetraodontidae) swim. Journal of Fish Biology 49:319–328.
Bray, D.J. (2024). Fishes of Australia: Whitespotted Eagle Ray. Museums Victoria and OzFishNet. Morphology, range and feeding; its older Vulnerable listing predates the 2024 IUCN update.

Status of Australian Fish Stocks (2023). Spotted Eagle Ray: habitat and size report. Its older global Vulnerable listing predates the 2024 IUCN Endangered assessment.
